source_refs.note: Topic 7.6 with Figs. 7.8 and 7.9, Examples 7.4 and 7.5 and the side boxes (PDF 150-155, printed 147-152). The print calls f3 = 3 f1 of a closed pipe the 'second harmonic'; recorded as a finding.

blocks.text: Stationary waves can also be set up in other media, such as an air column inside a pipe or tube; a common example of a vibrating air column is the organ pipe.

blocks.title: Organ pipe
blocks.text: An organ pipe is a wind instrument in which sound is produced by setting up stationary waves in an air column. It consists of a hollow long tube with both ends open, or with one end open and the other closed. The relationship between the incident wave and the reflected wave depends upon whether the reflecting end of the pipe is open or closed: if the reflecting end is open, the air molecules have complete freedom of motion and it behaves as an antinode; if the reflecting end is closed, it behaves as a node because the movement of the molecules is restricted.
Case 1: modes of vibration in an organ pipe open at both ends

Consider an organ pipe of length l open at both ends. As at an open end an air molecule has complete freedom of motion, it acts as an antinode (Fig. 7.8); the longitudinal waves set up inside the pipe are represented by transverse curved lines which show the displacement and amplitude of vibration of the air particles at various points along the axis of the pipe.

blocks.alt: Three pipes open at both ends, with shaded displacement envelopes. (a) one node in the middle, l = lambda1/2, f1 = v/2l; (b) two nodes, l = 2(lambda2/2), f2 = 2(v/2l); (c) three nodes, l = 3(lambda3/2), f3 = 3(v/2l). Above (a) and (b), green double arrows mark the antinodes and dots the nodes.
blocks.caption: Figure 7.8: Stationary longitudinal waves in a pipe open at both ends (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 7.8).

items: Fundamental mode (Fig. 7.8a): there is only one node N at the middle of the pipe, and antinodes at both open ends. If lambda1 is the wavelength of sound, l = lambda1/4 + lambda1/4 = lambda1/2, or lambda1 = 2l ... (7.7). If f1 is the frequency, v = f1 lambda1, so f1 = v/lambda1 = v/2l ... (7.8); this is the fundamental frequency or first harmonic.

Second mode (Fig. 7.8b): three antinodes and two nodes. If lambda2 is the wavelength, l = lambda2/4 + lambda2/2 + lambda2/4 = (1 + 2 + 1) lambda2/4, or lambda2 = l. Then v = f2 lambda2, f2 = v/lambda2 = v/l, or f2 = 2 f1 (since v/2l = f1).

nth mode: for the air column vibrating in n loops, fn = n (v/2l), fn = n f1, and lambda_n = 2l/n ... (7.9), where n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, ... So the longitudinal stationary waves have a discrete set of frequencies f1, 2f1, 3f1, ..., nf1, the harmonic series; f1 is the fundamental frequency and the others are called harmonics.

blocks.text: Case 2: modes of vibration in an organ pipe closed at one end
Consider an organ pipe of length l closed at one end. At the closed end we get a node, while at the open end we get an antinode (Fig. 7.9).

blocks.alt: Three pipes open at the left and closed at the right, with shaded displacement envelopes. (a) l = lambda1/4, f1 = v/4l; (b) l = 3(lambda3/4), f3 = 3(v/4l); (c) l = 5(lambda5/4), f5 = 5(v/4l). Above each, green double arrows mark the antinodes, the first at the open end, and dots the nodes, the last at the closed end.
blocks.caption: Figure 7.9: Stationary longitudinal waves in a pipe closed at one end. Only odd harmonics are present (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 7.9).

items: Fundamental mode (Fig. 7.9a): one node and one antinode. If lambda1 is the wavelength of the fundamental mode, the length of the pipe is l = lambda1/4, or lambda1 = 4l ... (7.10). The speed is v = f1 lambda1, so f1 = v/lambda1 = v/4l; f1 is the fundamental frequency.

Second mode of vibration (Fig. 7.9b): two nodes and two antinodes. If lambda3 is the wavelength, l = lambda3/4 + lambda3/2 = (3/4) lambda3, so lambda3 = 4l/3 ... (7.11). Putting this in v = f3 lambda3, f3 = v/(4l/3) = 3v/4l, so f3 = 3 f1 (since v/4l = f1). This is called second harmonic.
nth mode: if the air column vibrates in n loops, fn = n (v/4l), fn = n f1, and lambda_n = 4l/n ... (7.12), where n = 1, 3, 5, ... Only odd harmonics are present.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: f3 = 3 f1 is the third harmonic (harmonic number = f/f1 = 3); it is the second mode of vibration of a closed pipe, which has only odd harmonics.

By studying both cases we conclude that the pipe open at both ends is richer in harmonics than the pipe closed at one end: open pipes produce all harmonics, while closed pipes produce only odd harmonics (Ponder Upon). In an organ pipe the primary driving mechanism is a wavering, sheet-like jet of air from the flue-slit, which interacts with the upper lip and the air column in the pipe to maintain a steady oscillation (A Scientific Fact).

blocks.title: Example 7.4
blocks.text: An organ pipe has a length of 50 cm. Find the frequency of its fundamental note and the next harmonic when it is (a) open at both ends, (b) closed at one end (speed of sound = 350 m s^-1). Solution: l = 50 cm = 0.5 m, v = 350 m s^-1. (a) Open pipe: fn = n (v/2l), n = 1, 2, 3, ...; fundamental (n = 1) f1 = 1 x 350/(2 x 0.5) = 350 Hz; next harmonic (n = 2) f2 = 2v/2l = v/l = 350/0.5 = 700 Hz. (b) Closed at one end: fn = n (v/4l), n = 1, 3, 5, 7, ...; fundamental f1 = 1 x 350/(4 x 0.5) = 175 Hz; next harmonic (n = 3) f3 = 3v/4l = 3 x 350/(4 x 0.5) = 525 Hz.

blocks.title: Example 7.5
blocks.text: A church organ consists of pipes, each open at one end, of different lengths. The minimum length is 30 mm and the longest is 4 m. Calculate the frequency range of the fundamental notes (speed of sound = 340 m s^-1). Solution: l_min = 30 mm = 30 x 10^-3 m, l_max = 4 m, v = 340 m s^-1. For a pipe open at one end only, fn = nv/4l. (i) Minimum length, n = 1: f1,max = 1 x 340/(4 x 30 x 10^-3) = 2833.33 Hz. (ii) Maximum length, n = 1: f1,min = 1 x 340/(4 x 4) = 21.25 Hz. So the fundamental frequency range is approximately from 21 Hz to 2833 Hz.
